state.case_summary:
A 71-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of painful vision loss and floaters in her left eye. She had no history of myopia, ocular trauma, or surgery. Visual acuity was 20/30–2 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 21 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. The right eye was normal except for a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract and no inflammation. The left eye had rare anterior chamber cells, 1+ vitreous cells, choroidal detachments in the nasal and temporal periphery, and an overlying retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid; no retinal breaks were identified. Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, HIV, T-spot, syphilis screen, and ANCA panel) were normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed mild posterior scleral enhancement but no intraocular mass. Fluorescein angiography showed late leakage in the temporal periphery; fundus autofluorescence was normal; optical coherence tomography revealed shallow subretinal fluid and a posterior vitreous detachment. She was started on 80 mg oral prednisone for presumed serous retinal detachment secondary to posterior scleritis. Two weeks later, the choroidal detachments had resolved but the retinal detachment persisted and appeared more corrugated; intraocular pressures remained normal and no retinal breaks were seen.
